name: Principles of Economics for Public Policy
description:
1. How Economists think?
Your first module will focus on two topics: rational choice, and supply and demand. Based on the activities in this week, you can expect to be able to do the following:
• Discuss what the mainstream economic approach is, and evaluate potential applications and limitations of the theory of rational individual choice; and
• Differentiate some key concepts used by economists following this approach: demand, supply, and market equilibrium.
• What lies behind the Demand curve? (Utility curves, Budget constraints and the income and substitution effects)
• What lies behind the Supply curve? (Revenue, Costs, and Profit Maximization)
• Understanding the framework of perfectly competitive markets (revenues, costs, and profit maximization)
2. What to tax and why? 
There are two topics in this module: tax incidence and how to think of optimal taxes. Based on the activities in this week, you can expect to be able to do the following:
• Understand the concept of the economic incidence of a tax 
• Types of tax and role of demand elasticity
• how economists assess the ‘fairness’ of tax systems
3. What markets can achieve? 
The two topics in this module are: markets and efficiency, and trade. Based on the activities in this week, you can expect to be able to do the following:
• Understand the theory of comparative advantage and its implications for patterns of trade.
• Why competitive market outcomes are desirable (efficiency, pareto optimality, equity) 
4. Why markets may need regulation? 
(4.1): Natural monopolies and imperfect competition 
In this module, we will look at forms of imperfect competition when the number of sellers are limited, viz imperfect competition. We will use two case studies to motivate our learning: Electricity? And US versus Microsoft. Based on the activities in this week, you can expect to be able to do the following:
• Why monopoly (and market power more generally) may be “inefficient”? 
• The special case of Natural monopolies 
• Understand the effect of a small number of sellers on the market price and quantities supplied.
• Outline the range of policy responses to imperfect competition and the challenges of competition policy.
(4.2): Asymmetric information and the “lemons” problem 
In this module, we relax the assumption of full and common information for all participants in a market or allow for imperfect information. What happens to the market equilibrium now? Using a case study, Life Insurance, you can expect to be able to do the following:
• Be aware of different forms of asymmetric information and understand why these asymmetries may make markets inefficient. 
• Appreciate how private providers respond to asymmetric information, and 
• the extent to which policymakers can intervene to address this problem.
5. When can markets fail?
The Demand Supply framework breaks down in the case of certain types of goods. We discuss this with reference to the theory of goods noting the important category of public goods and common pool resources. 
• Policy interventions to supply public goods –e.g., defense expenditures and expenditures on primary education.
• Sometimes there may also be missing markets for external effects e.g. carbon taxes. 
• Positive externalities (peer learning effects, agglomeration economies)
• Appreciate the range of policy responses to external effects, including current debates concerning ways to reduce carbon emissions.
